issues.legal_issue: Succession to an impartible estate of a sovereign ruler follows primogeniture, and that rule continues after the ruler ceases to exercise sovereignty unless it is repealed.
material_facts: The ruling house followed primogeniture for succession to the Gaddi, with the eldest son succeeding as ruler.
The dispute concerned property said to form part of the estate of a former ruler, and the applicable succession rule was relevant to the competing claims of his heirs.
The court treated the rule of succession for an impartible ruler’s estate as continuing after the loss of sovereignty.
issues.conclusion: The rule of primogeniture applies to succession to the Gaddi of a sovereign ruler and continues to govern an impartible estate after the ruler ceases to be sovereign, unless repealed.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on Baboo Gunesh Dutt Singh v. Maharaja Moheshur Singh, the Digest of Customary Law in the Punjab, Jai Kaur v. Sher Singh, Salig Rain v. Maya Devi, Gopal Singh v. Ujagar Singh, the Privy Purses case, D.S. Meramwala Bhayavala v. Ba Shri Atarba Jethsurbhai, Thakore Shri Vinayasinghji v. Kumar Shri Natwarsinhji, and Rajkumar Narsingh Pratap Singh Deo v. State of Orissa. It held that primogeniture and impartibility are presumed for a sovereign ruler’s estate, and that the existing succession law continues under Article 372 of the Constitution. It also considered Section 5 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, which excludes certain estates descending to a single heir under a covenant or agreement.

rule.if: succession_to_former_ruler_estate_case and primogeniture_custom_applies and (estate_is_impartible or estate_is_held_as_sovereign_estate) and succession_rule_not_repealed

predicates.succession_to_former_ruler_estate_case: The proceeding concerns succession to the estate of a former ruler.
predicates.primogeniture_custom_applies: The ruling house followed a custom under which the eldest son succeeded to the rulership.
predicates.estate_is_impartible: The estate descends as a single estate rather than being divided among heirs.
predicates.estate_is_held_as_sovereign_estate: The estate was held by its ruler as part of the ruler’s sovereign estate.
predicates.succession_rule_not_repealed: No later law or other change had repealed the applicable succession rule.

issues.definition: When a succession proceeding concerns a former ruler’s estate, the house follows primogeniture, the estate is impartible or held as a sovereign estate, and the rule remains unrepealed, succession follows primogeniture.

issues.legal_issue: Property held by an absolute sovereign in the sovereign capacity is not subject to ordinary coparcenary rights arising by birth, and a separate capacity must be established to displace that treatment.
material_facts: The properties in dispute were acquired while the ruler exercised sovereign powers.
The court considered whether the ruler’s property should be divided into public and private property and whether the ruler’s sons acquired coparcenary interests in it by birth.
The court found that the ordinary incidents of ancestral coparcenary property were inconsistent with ownership by a sovereign ruler.
issues.conclusion: The ordinary distinction between public and private ownership does not apply to property held by an absolute sovereign merely because the property is described in one of those terms; a person asserting that the ruler held particular property in another capacity must establish that fact.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on Advocate General of Bombay v. Amerchund, Vishnu Pratap Singh v. State of M.P., Revathinnal Balagopala Varma v. His Highness Sri Padmanabha Dasa Bala Rama Varma, and D.S. Meramwala Bhayavala v. Ba Shri Atarba Jethsurbhai. It applied the principle that a sovereign ruler is the full owner of the estate held in the sovereign capacity and that ordinary coparcenary rights, including an interest by birth, do not arise in such an estate. A person asserting that the ruler held property in some other capacity must plead and establish that circumstance.

rule.if: sovereign_property_dispute and property_held_by_ruler_as_sovereign and not evidence_of_separate_capacity

predicates.sovereign_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns ownership of property held by a ruler.
predicates.property_held_by_ruler_as_sovereign: The ruler held the property in the exercise of sovereign authority.
predicates.evidence_of_separate_capacity: Evidence establishes that the ruler held the property in a capacity other than as sovereign.

issues.definition: Where a property dispute concerns property held by a ruler as sovereign and no evidence establishes a separate capacity, ordinary coparcenary rights by birth do not arise.

issues.legal_issue: A party asserting that property purchased in another person’s name was actually purchased for a ruler must prove the benami transaction, with the source of purchase money being the most important indicator.
material_facts: The heirs alleged that the ruler paid for the property from personal funds although the sale deed named another person as purchaser.
The evidence of personal funds and payment was principally oral, and the witness who described the payment could not support it with accounts or entries recording the transaction.

Contemporaneous records treated the property as belonging to the State, and the alleged relinquishment in favour of the heirs was not supported by the original document or testimony from a person connected with it.
issues.conclusion: The heirs failed to prove that the property was purchased benami for the ruler from his personal funds; the property was not his personal property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Jaydayal Poddar v. Mst Bibi Hazra, the burden of proving a benami transaction rests on the person asserting it and must be discharged by definite legal evidence. The court considered the source of purchase money, the nature and possession of the property, motive, the parties’ relationship, custody of title deeds, and the parties’ conduct, with the source of the purchase money being the most important indicator. It also referred to the factors stated in Mayne’s Hindu Law.

rule.if: partition_or_ownership_case and benami_purchase_is_alleged and state_ownership_records_exist and state_managed_or_used_property and not reliable_proof_of_personal_purchase_funds

predicates.partition_or_ownership_case: The proceeding seeks a share in or a determination of ownership of the disputed property.
predicates.benami_purchase_is_alleged: A claimant alleges that the named purchaser held the property for another person who supplied the purchase money.
predicates.state_ownership_records_exist: Contemporaneous records describe the property as belonging to the State.
predicates.state_managed_or_used_property: The State managed, possessed, leased, maintained, or otherwise dealt with the property as its own.
predicates.reliable_proof_of_personal_purchase_fund: Reliable evidence establishes that the alleged real owner supplied personal funds for the purchase.

issues.definition: In an ownership or partition proceeding, an alleged benami claim fails where State records and conduct show State ownership and reliable evidence does not establish payment from the alleged owner’s personal funds.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment concerning a different property and a materially different factual and legal issue does not operate as res judicata in a later property dispute.
material_facts: The earlier judgment concerned succession to a different estate and considered the character of funds used to purchase another property.
The present dispute concerned the ownership of a property acquired during the ruler’s exercise of sovereign powers.
The facts and the applicable law in the two proceedings were different.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgment of the Allahabad High Court did not constitute res judicata in the present dispute.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the doctrine of res judicata and held that the earlier judgment did not bar the present dispute because the facts and the law applicable to the two cases were materially different; the earlier finding concerned the character of particular funds and a separate property.

predicates.later_property_dispute_invokes_prior_jud: A party relies on an earlier judgment to prevent the court from deciding a later property dispute.
predicates.prior_case_concerned_different_property: The earlier judgment concerned ownership or succession relating to a different property.
predicates.prior_case_rest_on_materially_different_: The earlier judgment rested on facts or legal rules materially different from those in the later dispute.

issues.definition: An earlier judgment does not bar a later property dispute when it concerned a different property and rested on materially different facts or law.

issues.legal_issue: A property treated and administered as State property may be recognized as the ruler’s private property upon merger when the ruler includes it in the inventory and the covenanting authorities accept that classification.
material_facts: The property was bought in another person’s name and was treated for years as belonging to the State, including through State management, payment of expenses, leasing, and a formal release to the State.
After succeeding to the rulership, the ruler included the property in the inventory of properties he sought to retain as private property upon the State’s merger.
The authorities accepted the inventory and later records identified the property as the ruler’s private property.

The competing family claim that the property had remained the personal property of the former ruler was inconsistent with the contemporary records and with the claimant’s earlier assertion that the property had been given to her by the ruler.
issues.conclusion: The property was recognized as the ruler’s private property upon merger, and he was entitled to recover possession of it.
issues.legal_principle: Article VI of the covenant dealt with State assets, while Article XII entitled a ruler to retain private property belonging to him when administration was transferred and required an inventory of that property. The court held that the accepted recognition of the property as the ruler’s private property by the covenanting authorities amounted to an act of State. It rejected the contention that the ruler’s inclusion of the property could be disregarded in light of the State’s prior records and conduct, and relied on the rule against acquiring immovable property in British territory by a ruling chief, which explained the use of a benamidar.

predicates.possession_recovery_case: The proceeding seeks recovery of possession of property from persons occupying or claiming it.
predicates.property_was_acquired_and_administered_a: The property was acquired in another person’s name but was managed, maintained, leased, or recorded as belonging to the State.
predicates.ruler_included_property_in_private_inven: The ruler included the property in an inventory of property he sought to retain as private property when the State’s administration was transferred.
predicates.covenanting_authorities_accepted_invento: The authorities responsible for the merger accepted the inventory and recognized the property as the ruler’s private property.

issues.definition: Where a ruler seeks possession of property administered as a State asset but included it in an inventory accepted by the merger authorities as his private property, the recognized ruler-owner is entitled to possession.
